summary: Portland Breakwater Light (Bug Light), a pier light at the end of Portland Harbor's breakwater: 1855 wooden tower, 1875 iron tower, darkened 1942, relit as a private aid in 2002.

lens.where: sixth-order lens at the South Portland Coast Guard Station (LighthouseFriends)

structures.note: Small octagonal wooden tower on two courses of ashlar; moved to Little Diamond Island as a lookout after 1875 (LighthouseFriends; New England Lighthouses).

Cast-iron plates fashioned as fluted columns with Corinthian capitals; brick filling inside; design based on the Choragic Monument of Lysicrates (NRHP; LighthouseFriends). Height: 26 ft (LighthouseFriends); 24 ft to the lantern tip (New England Lighthouses).
Annex to the tower with two dwelling rooms (Board 1889, as quoted by LighthouseFriends); attic and rooms added 1903; removed 1935.
Bell house to shelter a 1,000-pound bell that replaced a 400-pound bell (LighthouseFriends).

access.note: Bug Light Park; grounds open, tower closed; the short breakwater can be walked to the light (LighthouseFriends). USLHS: open to the public.

facts.agency: City of South Portland owns the lighthouse; lit as a private aid to navigation since 2002

events.note: Storm ravages Portland Harbor, the reason for the breakwater
Lighthouse Board petitions Congress for $3,500 for a light on the breakwater
Appropriation of $3,500 made on 3 August 1854
Small octagonal wooden tower into service on 1 August 1855 with a sixth-order Fresnel lens
Sixth-order Fresnel lens, fixed red light 25 ft above high water
Breakwater extended (completed September 1873); wooden tower placed at the end of the extended breakwater
Congress appropriates $6,000 to replace the wooden tower
Cast-iron tower built
New iron tower first lit in June 1875 by Keeper Stephen Hubbard
Wooden tower moved to Little Diamond Island, lookout at a buoy depot
Fixed red changed to a red flash every fifteen seconds (LighthouseFriends)
Iron handrail along the breakwater
Two-room dwelling annex built beside the tower
Staniford Ledge bell buoy, 24 June 1895, operated electrically from the light station
Staniford Ledge fog bell removed to the light for the winter, 20 January 1896; back on the buoy 16 May 1896
Electric motor and machinery installed to strike the fog bell
Stevens striking machine replaces the electric machine for the fog bell
Bell house built for a 1,000-pound bell
District inspector's letter about the fog bell not sounding during thick fog (3:44 a.m. complaint from the steamer Bay State)
Light electrified and operated by remote control from the Spring Point Ledge keeper
Keeper's dwelling on the breakwater removed (late February 1935)
Light darkened; discontinued June 1942 (LighthouseFriends; USLHS gives 1942-2002)
May 1943: decided the light and fog signal were no longer needed for local navigation
Listed on the National Register of Historic Places (NRHP reference 73000238)
Property donated by Spring Point Associates to the City of South Portland
Renovation led by the South Portland–Cape Elizabeth Rotary Club
Relighted as a private aid to navigation, 14 August 2002, with a 250 mm optic

corrections.proposed: City of South Portland (owner); private aid to navigation since 2002
corrections.why: USLHS and LighthouseFriends both give the City of South Portland as owner; USLHS marks the light as a private aid. The Coast Guard appears only as the former federal owner.
The standing tower is the 1875 cast-iron tower; the 1855 wooden tower was moved to Little Diamond Island. The record's 7.5 m tower matches the 1875 structure.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: USLHS marks the light not an active aid (Private Aid: Yes). LighthouseFriends and New England Lighthouses report it relit as a private aid to navigation on 14 August 2002, showing a white flash every four seconds, so it is lit.
The 1855 date is the first wooden light, which went into service on 1 August 1855; the present iron tower dates from 1875 (first lit June 1875).
LighthouseFriends: first section begun in summer 1836; New England Lighthouses: construction began in 1837. Stated in the story.

The NRHP nomination says the structure was first built in 1855 and rebuilt in 1875, and its physical description gives 1855 for the cast-iron tower; LighthouseFriends and NEL date the cast-iron tower to 1875 and the wooden light to 1855. Stated in the story.

LighthouseFriends describes an onshore keeper's residence torn down in 1871 and rebuilt; the Board's 1889 report (as LighthouseFriends quotes it) says the station had no provision for a keeper's dwelling. Stated in the story.
USLHS 1909-1919; NEL 1910-1919. Stated in the story.

notes_for_editor: (1) NRHP OCR: the date of abandonment in the statement of significance is garbled ('19^3^'); the story uses 1942 (LighthouseFriends, USLHS 1942-2002, New England Lighthouses 'darkened in 1942') and May 1943 (New England Lighthouses). Check the scan. (2) Tower height: LighthouseFriends 26 ft; New England Lighthouses 24 ft to lantern tip; record 7.5 m; USLHS gives 13 ft for both measures, which looks wrong for the iron tower; not used. (3) Focal height: record 9.1 m; LighthouseFriends 25 ft in 1855; USLHS 13 ft for the current light; left out. (4) Keeper's dwelling before 1889: LighthouseFriends says an onshore keeper's residence was torn down in 1871 and replaced; the Board's 1889 report (as quoted by LighthouseFriends) says the station had no provision for a dwelling; New England Lighthouses says none until 1889. Not resolved; the story follows the Board. (5) Holbrook: USLHS 1909-1919; New England Lighthouses 1910-1919. (6) Fog bell dates to the light: LighthouseFriends 1896 electric striking and 1898 permanent; New England Lighthouses 1897 relocation; the Board's reports (1896-1897, 1899) are used. (7) Thomas Ustick Walter: the nomination says 'possible' only; New England Lighthouses says 'suggested'; the story repeats it as a possibility. (8) The Board's 1853 petition and 1889 report are quoted as LighthouseFriends quotes them; neither report is in the local corpus. (9) Chronicling America searches for wrecks and rescues at the light gave only noisy OCR hits; no wreck or rescue is written. (10) Al Glickman is not named (New England Lighthouses names him); the donor is given as Spring Point Associates. Keepers' family members in NEL are not named. (11) The NEL account of the 1914 letter quotes a National Archives letter we did not read; the quoted sentence is as NEL prints it. (12) Printed page numbers were not read; citations use Internet Archive scan pages. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-22 (Haiku fact-checker): (a) Board volume labels: the two 1896 citations (scan 34 and 53) are in the fiscal-1896 report, which opens that volume; the Stevens striking machine (scan 81) is in the fiscal-1899 report. (b) The 1895 bell-buoy entry (scan 27) is in the fiscal-1895 report, which opens that volume. (c) 'Staniford Ledge' is the Board's spelling (1895 and 1896 reports); New England Lighthouses writes 'Stanford Ledge' and LighthouseFriends 'Staniford'. (d) The 1914 Holbrook letter: NEL gives the keeper's bell hours as 7:30 to 10:30 p.m. with the weather clear at 11:00 p.m.; the earlier draft's timing is corrected. (e) Unresolved: height (LighthouseFriends 26 ft; NEL 24 ft to lantern tip; the Archive's 13 ft looks wrong for the iron tower). The story gives no height. (f) The NRHP's 'abandoned in 19^3^' is garbled in OCR; 1942 comes from LighthouseFriends, the Archive (1942-2002) and NEL. (g) Units added to the breakwater length, the focal height, the tower's width and the brick filler.
